title: Two faces of every action
goal: Recognize *vid* (aspect) — the fact that almost every Bosnian verb comes in two forms, one for an action in progress and one for a completed action — and know which to use when.
bekal: recognizing *vid* pairs and noting down new verbs in pairs
choosing the *nesvršeni* (imperfective) form for processes and habits, *svršeni* (perfective) for results
understanding why the perfective in the present tense actually points to the future

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jesi li pročitao knjigu?
dialogs.intro: Amina lent Budi a novel two weeks ago, and today she wants it back — half joking.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Budi, jesi li pročitao onu knjigu koju sam ti dala?
lines.id: Budi, have you finished that book I gave you?
lines.literal: Budi, you-are whether read-through-m that-acc-f book which-acc-f I-am to-you given-f?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Čitao sam je, ali nisam je pročitao. Teška je.
lines.id: I've been reading it, but I haven't finished it. It's heavy going.
lines.literal: read-m I-am it-acc, but I-am-not it-acc read-through-m. heavy-f it-is.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: How many pages have you read?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pedeset. Čitam svako veče po malo.
lines.id: Fifty. I read a little every evening.
lines.literal: fifty. I-read every-n evening by little.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: To je dobro. A jesi li napisao izvještaj?
lines.id: That's good. And have you finished writing the report?
lines.literal: that it-is good. and you-are whether written-through-m report-acc?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pisao sam ga cijelo popodne, ali još nije gotov.
lines.id: I was writing it all afternoon, but it's not done yet.
lines.literal: written-m I-am it-acc whole-n afternoon, but still not-it-is finished-m.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ha! Znači, radio si, ali nisi uradio.
lines.id: Ha! So you worked on it, but you didn't get it done.
lines.literal: ha! means, worked-m you-are, but you-are-not done-m.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tačno tako. Bosanski me je naučio jednoj stvari.
lines.id: Exactly. Bosnian has taught me one thing.
lines.literal: exactly so. Bosnian me-acc it-is taught-m one-dat-f thing-dat.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Sad si pravi Bosanac. Jesi li kupio kafu?
lines.id: Now you're a real Bosnian. Did you buy the coffee?
lines.literal: now you-are real-m Bosnian. you-are whether bought-m coffee-acc?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kupovao sam je jučer, ali nisam kupio — nije bilo u prodavnici.
lines.id: I tried to buy it yesterday, but didn't manage — the shop was out.
lines.literal: buying-m I-am it-acc yesterday, but I-am-not bought-m — not-it-is been-n in shop-loc.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Then let's go get coffee. Right now.

notes: ***Čitao sam, ali nisam pročitao* — one sentence that sums up this whole unit.** The first verb says **the process happened**; the second says **the result was not reached**. English does the same thing with tenses and extra words ("I was reading" vs "I've finished reading"); Bosnian does it with two different verbs.
***Radio si, ali nisi uradio*** is a joke that only works in Slavic languages — "you worked, but you didn't get it done". If you can see why that sentence is funny, you already understand *vid*.

***Kupovao sam, ali nisam kupio*** shows the same thing with a verb whose partner isn't just a prefix: *kupovati* (be shopping, try to buy) vs *kupiti* (succeed in buying). Pairs where the stem changes like this have to be learned whole.

***Po malo* means "a little at a time".** The preposition *po* is used for sharing out: *po malo* (bit by bit), *po jedan* (one each, one by one), *dva puta po sat* (twice for an hour), *po osobi* (per person).

**A consolation.** Even native speakers sometimes hesitate over the right aspect for a rarely used verb, and a wrong choice **almost never makes your sentence impossible to understand** — it just sounds a little off. So don't hold back from speaking until you've mastered it; what matters is starting to note verbs down in pairs from today.

grammars.title: Dva vida — and how the pairs are formed
body: Almost every action in Bosnian has two verbs: **nesvršeni** (imperfective — a process, a habit, an ongoing state) and **svršeni** (perfective — one complete action, with a result).
after: **A prefix doesn't always just mean "finish" — sometimes it changes the meaning.** *Pisati* (write) → *napisati* (finish writing), but also *potpisati* (sign), *prepisati* (copy), *opisati* (describe), *zapisati* (note down). All are perfective verbs, but their meanings differ. This is how Bosnian grows its vocabulary: one stem, a dozen prefixes.

**When a prefix changes the meaning, Bosnian makes yet another pair** by lengthening the stem: *potpisati* (perfective) pairs with *potpisivati* (imperfective). You don't need to build these yourself yet; just know that the endings *-ivati* and *-avati* almost always mark an imperfective form.

**Some verbs have no partner at all**, because their meaning can't be "finished": *biti* (be), *imati* (have), *moći* (can), *znati* (know), *voljeti* (love), *živjeti* (live). It's a small group, and they're all verbs of state.

**The right way to learn from today on:** note verbs down **in pairs**, not one by one. Not *čitati*, but *čitati / pročitati*. It's the biggest investment you can make before A2, because the whole past and future depend on it.

grammars.title: Which one when
body: Three rules cover almost every situation you'll meet at A1.

head: Situation
Aspect
Example
Meaning
rows: When I've finished, I'll let you know.

after: **The single most important rule: a *svršeni* form NEVER means "now".** *Čitam* = I'm reading; *pročitam* does **not** mean "I'm finishing reading" but something that hasn't happened yet. That's why *pročitam* almost always appears after *kada* (when), *ako* (if), or as part of the future.

**Negation brings the difference to the surface.** *Nisam čitao knjigu* = I didn't read the book at all. *Nisam pročitao knjigu* = I read some of it, but didn't finish. One prefix, two very different pieces of news — and this is where the choice of aspect really matters.

**Adverbs are often a clue.** *Cijeli dan, često, obično, svaki dan, dugo* pull toward the imperfective. *Odjednom, konačno, brzo, jednom* pull toward the perfective. If in doubt, look at the time expression first.

**A self-check:** ask "does this sentence have an end point?" *Jučer sam pisao* (yesterday I was writing — finished or not, who knows) vs *Jučer sam napisao pismo* (yesterday the letter got written). If there's a result you could point to, use the perfective.

sections.title: The aspect pairs you'll need most

blocks.text: Thirty pairs that cover almost all everyday conversation. Copy them into your notes as pairs — the first two columns, always side by side.

blocks.title: One stem, a dozen words
items: From *pisati* (write) come: *napisati* (finish writing), *potpisati* (sign), *prepisati* (copy), *zapisati* (note down), *opisati* (describe), *upisati* (enroll, enter), *ispisati* (write out in full), *raspisati* (announce). Eight verbs from one stem.

From *ići* (go) come: *doći* (come), *otići* (go away), *ući* (enter), *izaći* (go out), *proći* (pass), *naći* (find), *preći* (cross), *sići* (go down). Notice that the stem changes its sound, but the *-ći* pattern is still visible.

This is why Bosnian vocabulary grows much faster than you'd expect: once you recognize the stem, you can guess the meaning of words you've never seen. The most common prefixes: *do-* (up to, arrive), *iz-* (out), *na-* (on, finished), *o-* (around), *od-* (away), *po-* (briefly, finished), *pre-* (across, again), *pri-* (toward), *u-* (in), *za-* (start, closed).
